claims.text: Compositional complexity enhances the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys.
Compositional complexity drives selective surface segregation of protective elements such as Cr and Al during high-temperature exposure.
Selective segregation of Cr and Al leads to formation and retention of a continuous, adherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer.
The initial high-entropy alloy is homogeneously mixed with a nearly uniform distribution of all constituent elements.
High-entropy alloys possess sluggish diffusion arising from their compositionally complex matrices.
Sluggish diffusion enhances in-situ surface segregation of protective elements.
Segregation of protective elements produces a densely packed and stable oxide scale.
Multiple principal elements and associated lattice distortions slow bulk diffusion in high-entropy alloys.
The slowed bulk diffusion enables selective migration of oxidation-prone elements such as Cr and Al to the surface.
Surface-enriched Cr and Al form protective oxides that adhere strongly.
The protective oxides limit further oxidation and retard oxide-scale growth relative to less compositionally complex alloys.

Under matched oxidation conditions, the high-entropy alloy will develop a higher surface concentration of Cr and/or Al than a conventional alloy of similar average composition but lower elemental complexity.
The high-entropy alloy will form an oxide layer that is thinner, more uniform, and more resistant to further oxidation than the baseline alloy's scale.
The lower-complexity baseline alloy is expected to exhibit less selective surface segregation.
The lower-complexity baseline alloy is expected to develop a thicker, less uniform, and more rapidly growing oxide scale.
The proposed effect requires temperatures high enough to activate diffusion.
At lower temperatures where diffusion is minimal, segregation and protective-oxide formation will be less pronounced.
